name: method-object
intent: Turn one method invocation into a short-lived object whose fields are the method's receiver, arguments and former local variables, so a long method with entangled locals can be decomposed into small methods that share state through the object instead of through parameter lists.
problem: A method has grown too long to read, and its local variables are so intertwined - each assigned in one place and read or updated in several others - that Extract Method cannot be applied without threading an unwieldy set of parameters and return values between the pieces. The computation needs its own state, and the host class must not accumulate helper methods that only this one method calls.
context: Applies where one algorithm of a single invocation owns a cohesive set of mutable intermediates and the host object has no natural home for the extracted steps: pricing and valuation, parsers, layout and geometry, report generation, simulation step functions, and legacy procedural methods being untangled. It matters most where the language cannot let several closures share one mutable state (Java's effectively-final capture rule) or where the extracted algorithm must be named, unit-tested and reused in isolation.
benefits: Unlocks decomposition: once the locals are fields, every step method can read and write them without a parameter list, so a 150-line body becomes a dozen named methods at one level of abstraction.
The algorithm becomes a named, testable unit: the method object can be instantiated directly from a test with a few values instead of driving the host object through a long setup.
The host class stays clean: helpers, constants and intermediate types that belong only to this computation live in the new class instead of polluting the original type's interface and its subclasses.
The refactoring is incremental and behaviour-preserving: the body is copied once, then Extract Method is applied repeatedly with tests run after each step.
The extracted object is a natural seed for later evolution - turning into a Strategy implementation, a Command, or a parameter object - without another restructuring pass.
tradeoffs: An extra type and an extra allocation per invocation: negligible in ordinary code, visible in a hot loop that could have been served by passing a small parameter tuple.
Indirection: readers must jump to another type to follow the algorithm, and a poorly named class (OrderHelper, UtilCalculator) costs more comprehension than the long method it replaced.
The object can degenerate into a state machine: promoting every temporary to a field creates a class whose invariants are unclear and whose methods must be called in a particular order.

Encapsulation can be damaged by the refactoring itself: if the algorithm needs the host's private members, extraction forces package-private or protected accessors, coupling the two classes (or duplicating logic).
Per-invocation state must stay per-invocation: nothing prevents reusing one instance for a second computation, which silently carries the previous call's values.
Over-application: used where plain Extract Method or a Parameter Object would do, it multiplies types and moves the code farther from the data it operates on.

participants.responsibility: The original long method, reduced to a one-line delegation that constructs the method object (with the receiver and the arguments) and calls its entry method.
Holds the original receiver, the arguments and the former local variables as fields, and exposes exactly one public entry point (compute/execute/call) that runs the algorithm.
The private methods the algorithm is decomposed into; they share the object's fields instead of taking parameters, which is the decomposition that was impossible in the host method.
The object whose data and behaviour the algorithm needs; held as a field (or passed as the values it provides) so the method object does not duplicate the host's state.
Accepts the receiver and the arguments and initialises every field, so the invocation contract is explicit and the object is usable only in one fully initialised state.

use_cases: A pricing or valuation method (Order.price()) with a dozen base-price temporaries, several discount rules and a final rounding step.
A parser loop whose token position, lookahead and accumulator locals are threaded through many branches and need to be split into named steps.
Legacy procedural code being untangled: a 300-line process() that validates, transforms and assembles over a dozen locals.
A simulation or animation step function that computes one frame with many intermediate vectors and scalars.
A fat service method inside a class that must not grow more private helpers (published or already oversized type), where the computation deserves its own type.
Geometry, layout or report-generation algorithms with scratch state that must be unit-tested against known inputs.
A compiler function-lowering pass in Clang/LLVM: CodeGenFunction owns per-function builder, current-function, loop and cleanup state while helper methods emit one function.
Rustc's MIR backend uses a FunctionCx per function to carry the MIR body, backend function, block caches, cleanup state and locals while helper methods lower it.
SQLAlchemy Core's SQLCompiler encapsulates per-statement dialect, statement and compile-state data while process() helpers render nested SQL expressions.
avoid_when: The method is merely long but separable: apply Extract Method (towards a Composed Method) first, and reach for a method object only when parameters and return values block the extraction.
The locals travel together as one cohesive concept: introduce a Parameter Object or a value type instead of a class that also owns the algorithm.
The step results can be threaded as values (small pure functions): plain functions or closures are simpler than a stateful object.
The method is long because it does several unrelated things: split it by responsibility into collaborators, not into a single algorithm object.

The language has nested functions that capture and mutate locals (Python, JavaScript, Ruby, Kotlin, Swift, Scala, C#, Go): a set of local steps is usually enough; extract a named class only when the computation must be tested, reused or documented as a unit.
anti_patterns: God method object: every temporary promoted to a field and dozens of public methods, with the algorithm's real state machine hidden in call order.
Widening the host's private API just to feed the method object, coupling the two classes for the sake of a refactoring that was supposed to improve structure.
Caching or reusing one method-object instance across invocations, so state bleeds between calls.
Naming the class after the mechanism (OrderHelper, CalculationUtil) rather than the computation (PriceCalculator), adding navigation cost without meaning.
Extracting a method object for one method while leaving the class's other 300-line methods untouched: a new type instead of a decomposition habit.
design_principles: Composed Method / single level of abstraction: the entry method reads as a sequence of named steps, and each step is one level down.
Separation of concerns: the algorithm's working state and steps belong to the computation, not to the host object's identity.
Single responsibility: one class per computation; the host keeps only delegation.
Encapsulation and information hiding: the method object's state stays private to the computation and the host exposes no new API.
Behaviour-preserving transformation: the refactoring is applied in verified steps, tests running after each extraction.
best_practices: Copy the body once into the entry method, run the tests, then apply Extract Method step by step, re-running them after each step.
Name the class after what it computes (PriceCalculator, TaskSender, LineParser), never after the host or a generic helper.
Keep exactly one public entry point and make every step private; the constructor is the invocation contract.
Hold the receiver as a field only if the algorithm genuinely needs it, and pass values rather than exposing host internals.
Promote a temporary to a field only when two or more step methods need it (pull, do not push: keep it local as long as possible).
Create a new instance per invocation, and keep the host method a one-line delegator so the entry point's contract stays visible.
Test the method object directly with small inputs; that is where the extracted algorithm's boundary conditions belong.
sources: Beck, Smalltalk Best Practice Patterns (1997) - Method Object (Patterns/Methods section): create a class named after the method, an instance variable for the receiver, each argument and each temporary, one #compute method, and replace the original method with a creation-and-compute call.
Fowler, Refactoring: Improving the Design of Existing Code (1999) - Replace Method with Method Object; renamed Replace Function with Command in the 2nd edition (2018).
